description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes apasionados por la tecnología, la ciencia y la innovación. Nuestro objetivo es desarrollar una solución basada en datos abiertos de la NASA para analizar cambios ambientales relacionados con el fenómeno de El Niño. Buscamos transformar información científica en herramientas útiles, accesibles y con impacto real en la sociedad, combinando creatividad, programación, investigación y trabajo en equipo.
summary: NiñoLab is a web platform that investigates environmental change like a scientist and explains it like a teacher. A user asks a question, for example "How have rainfall patterns changed in Piura?", and NiñoLab retrieves NASA POWER time series (1981–2025), analyzes the full period, and tests whether a trend is real using the Mann-Kendall test, Sen's slope and a robustness check. It then reports one of three evidence states: supported change, insufficient evidence, or inconclusive. Results appear first in plain language, then as interactive charts and a verifiable scientific file. Interactive maps show Peru's departments and NASA satellite imagery of the Pacific, with a coastal index for El Niño. NiñoLab answers the challenge's questions (what, where, how much, is it significant) and adds a fifth: what it means for people.
details:
THE PROBLEM

El Niño has repeatedly hit Peru's coast (1983, 1998, 2017, 2023). NASA publishes open Earth data, but farmers, fishers, livestock keepers and small businesses rarely can read anomalies, units or statistical tests. A rising line on a chart does not tell them whether it is a real trend or a single exceptional year.

WHAT NIÑOLAB DOES

NiñoLab turns NASA data into verified, understandable discoveries. Every investigation follows one flow: question → NASA data request → coverage and quality check → full-period analysis → trend verification → plain-language explanation.

- My profile: three questions, no login (sector, department, main concern). The profile adapts explanations and suggestions, never the scientific results.

- Investigate: pulls NASA POWER series (rainfall, air temperature, soil wetness, surface temperature) from 1981. It compares against a 1991–2020 baseline, splits the period into three equal stages, flags exceptional years, and runs Mann-Kendall (with autocorrelation correction), Sen's slope and a test without the two most extreme years. Results come in three levels: Understand, Explore and Verify, with a copyable JSON file of the series, tests and conclusion.

- Territory: interactive map of Peru's 25 departments with five layers (rain, clouds, humidity, temperature, wind), color legends, an hour slider and department comparison.

- Ocean: NASA GIBS satellite layers of the Pacific (sea surface temperature and anomaly from NASA/JPL MUR, sea level anomaly, currents and salinity). Users click any point to read its value, compare two coastal locations, and see the Niño 3.4, 3 and 1+2 regions. A coastal index for the Niño 1+2 region, computed by our team from NASA POWER, is shown with historical series and episode comparison.

- El Niño in Peru: a timeline from 1578 to today. The final "in progress" entry is built from the live index.

- My findings: investigations saved in the user's browser.

- Duke, our assistant: explains the current result using the numbers the engine computed, and answers concept questions with fixed, reviewed answers. It does not generate data.

SCIENTIFIC INTEGRITY

NiñoLab separates anomaly, trend, statistical significance and practical relevance. It says "insufficient evidence" instead of overclaiming: in our Piura rainfall test (1981–2025) it reports no supported sustained trend because the result depends heavily on the exceptional year 1998. It never presents a historical trend as a forecast and does not predict El Niño. Every result shows its source, period and limitations. Example series are used only when there is no connection, and they are clearly labeled.

LIMITATIONS

NASA POWER values are a reanalysis cell of about 50 km, not a departmental average. Territory colors show today's weather (Open-Meteo), not NASA imagery. Some GIBS layers (sea level, currents) are not updated daily; the page shows each layer's date. Our coastal index is not the official ICEN from ENFEN.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

NiñoLab reduces uncertainty for people who make decisions about land, water, livestock, fishing and tourism, and helps them prepare earlier. It also teaches: each result explains how it was checked. The same approach can be extended to other regions where compatible NASA data exist.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework), Leaflet for maps, SVG and Canvas for charts and the interactive globe. Data through NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS (WMTS) and Open-Meteo. Hosted on GitHub Pages. Pitch video built with Remotion. Source code: https://github.com/aguirre2iq/NinoLab

CREATIVITY

A "detective" approach with three evidence states, a three-level explanation (Understand, Explore, Verify), a profile that changes the explanation but not the science, an interactive globe, and Duke as a guide.

NEXT STEPS

Move the analysis engine to a Java 21 / Spring Boot backend with a React frontend, add GPM IMERG, MODIS and SMAP soil moisture, integrate the official ICEN/ONI indices, and include validated forecast products with their uncertainty.

TEAM

Three students: one in Systems Engineering, one in Industrial Engineering, and one in Administration.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) DISCLOSURE

We used Anthropic's Claude (through Claude Code) to help write the website code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), draft interface text and documentation, and prepare this submission. The pitch video's animation code, voice-over and music were generated with SI tools, and the video carries a visible SI watermark. The scientific methods, data sources and design requirements were specified by our team. No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers are used.
